rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes `float accum[4][4]` to `float accum[5][4]`. All loops accessing accum are bounded by `i < 4` and `j < 4`. The update loop (lines ~89-97) iterates `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` and `for (int j = 0; j < 4; j++)`, only writing to accum[0..3][0..3]. The write-results loop (lines ~103-114) similarly only reads accum[0..3][0..3]. The extra row accum[4][*] is allocated but never accessed.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation adds an extra row to the accumulator array (changing dimensions from 4x4 to 5x4), but this extra row at index 4 is never written to or read from during kernel execution. Both the computation loop that updates the accumulator (`for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)`) and the final write loop that copies results to global memory use the same bounds `i < 4`. Since all array accesses use indices in the range [0,3], the extra memory at index 4 has no functional impact. The C++ initialization `{{0.0f}}` zero-initializes all elements in both the original and mutated versions. This is dead memory allocation that cannot affect output.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable because it is semantically equivalent. The extra row accum[4][*] is never accessed by any code path regardless of input values. No value-level test can distinguish the outputs since the same computation is performed with the same data.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should detect 'dead allocation' mutations where array dimensions are increased beyond what loop bounds access. Static analysis could verify that all array index expressions have upper bounds strictly less than the new dimension, flagging such mutations as equivalent before dynamic testing.
